alt: Two equations. Narration equals story (details about a real-life experience) plus significance (reflection on what it means). Cause-effect equals links (a cause and effects, a chain, or several causes) plus reasoning (evidence of how one leads to another). Notes warn what happens with only half.
caption: Narration needs story plus significance; cause-effect needs links plus reasoning.

alt: Five features of effective narration with the Harbour Road bus-stop examples: specific detail, selection, sequence, perspective and reflection. A bar shows narration working best to open an argument, illustrate a claim midway, or close by returning to the opening story.
caption: Specific, selected, ordered detail, then reflection that states the significance.

alt: Three diagrams. One cause with several effects: a bridge closure leads to longer bus routes and fewer clinic visits. A chain: later closing times reduce the homework club, then coursework marks, then the number who qualify. Several causes, one effect: rising rents, falling footfall and the loss of the market together empty the high street.
caption: One cause with effects, a chain of consequences, or many causes behind one effect.

alt: An arrow from A to B with a question mark, and four questions for any causal link: is there evidence of the connection, could something else explain it, is the effect proportionate, and is the writer clear about strength? Below, “may have led to”, “contributed to” and “caused” form a scale of certainty.
caption: A causal claim is only as strong as its weakest link; match your verbs to the evidence.

alt: A chain of four events from a story: the bus was late, so I missed the interview, so the job went to someone else, so a timetable decided my year. Below, the reflection states the general claim: unreliable buses change the course of people’s lives.
caption: The story shows the chain at work; the reflection states the claim it supports.

after: ## A public-domain example of cause-effect: Wollstonecraft (1792)
alt: Wollstonecraft’s sentence is split into a cause, strengthening and enlarging women’s minds, and an effect, an end to blind obedience. A second causal claim follows: because power seeks blind obedience, those with power oppose education.
caption: Condition and consequence present reform as something readers can cause.

after: ## Worked example 2: analysing a cause-effect chain
alt: The evening-bus chain as six linked steps from the cut in March to the claim that it cost the town far more. Notes rate each link: the first is supported by a reason and data, the next two rest on assumptions or unquantified claims, and the final conclusion is overstated.
caption: Test every link: a chain is only as strong as its weakest, least-evidenced step.
